title: Statistics - Lesson 3: Claims and Displays Assessment
description: Assessment on judging statistical claims, displays, scales, sources, and evidence-based conclusions.

questions.question: Which question best begins a check of any statistical claim?
options: What exactly is the claim saying?
How bright are the graph colors?
Can the graph fit on one page?
Does the conclusion sound confident?
questions.explanation: You must identify the exact claim before deciding which evidence would support it.

questions.question: A survey found that 27 out of 45 students use video lessons. What percent is this? Enter a percent such as 60%.
A report claims, "Attendance steadily increased all week." Which display would best support that claim?
options: A line graph of attendance by day
A pie chart of favorite subjects
A bar graph with no labels
A table showing only Friday attendance
questions.explanation: A line graph by day can show whether the values increased steadily over time.

questions.question: If a graph has clear labels and a source, you should still check whether the scale exaggerates differences.
questions.explanation: Labels and source help, but scale can still affect how large a pattern appears.

questions.question: A class has 12 students who chose A, 10 who chose B, and 8 who chose C. Which claim is supported?
options: A was the most selected option
Most students chose A
Almost everyone chose A
No one chose C
questions.explanation: A has the highest count, but 12 out of 30 is only 40%, so it is not most or almost everyone.

questions.question: A graph shows test averages of 86 and 88, but the y-axis runs only from 84 to 89. Explain why the display may be misleading.
questions.correctAnswer: The shortened y-axis can make the 2-point difference look much larger than it is.
questions.explanation: The values may be correct, but the scale visually exaggerates a small difference.

questions.question: Which detail most directly helps you decide whether a survey represents all Grade 10 students?
options: How the students were selected
The font used in the title
The number of colors in the graph
Whether the bars are vertical or horizontal
questions.explanation: Sampling method affects whether the data fairly represent the group named in the claim.

questions.question: Section A has 19 club members and Section B has 26. How many more club members does Section B have? Enter just the number.
A data set is 60, 62, 63, 64, 99. Which statistic may better describe a typical value if the claim should avoid the outlier's effect?
options: Median
Maximum only
Range only
Sample size only
questions.explanation: The median resists the effect of the high outlier 99 better than the mean.

questions.question: A conclusion should be limited to the group and data that were actually studied.
questions.explanation: Statistical conclusions should not generalize beyond the data source without evidence that the sample represents the larger group.

questions.question: A table says 31 of 40 students passed. Which wording is best supported?
options: Most students in the surveyed group passed
Every student mastered the lesson
Nearly no one had difficulty
The lesson guarantees passing
questions.explanation: 31 out of 40 is 77.5%, so most passed, but the stronger claims are not supported.

questions.question: A school announcement says, "Students prefer digital assignments," but gives no counts or percentages. What evidence would you ask for?
questions.correctAnswer: I would ask for the number or percent who preferred digital assignments, the total surveyed, and how the students were selected.
questions.explanation: Counts, total sample size, and sampling method help judge whether the claim is supported and representative.

questions.question: Which claim is best supported by a pie chart or percent bar?
options: About one-fourth of the class chose option D
The quiz average increased each week
The median score was 82
Scores are spread from 50 to 100
questions.explanation: Pie charts and percent bars are useful for showing parts of a whole.

questions.question: Write a careful conclusion for this evidence: In a survey of 100 Grade 10 students, 54 preferred group review, 31 preferred video lessons, and 15 preferred printed notes.
questions.correctAnswer: In this survey of 100 Grade 10 students, group review was the most preferred option and was chosen by a small majority, 54%.
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion names the group, gives the key value, and avoids extending the claim beyond the survey.

questions.question: Explain the difference between "the largest category" and "most of the group" in a statistical claim.
questions.correctAnswer: The largest category has more responses than any other single category, while most of the group means more than half of the total.
questions.explanation: This distinction prevents overclaiming when the top category is still less than 50%.
